The rain fell in sheets against the cabin windows, each drop a tiny percussionist hammering out a rhythm only the lonely could hear. I sat by the fire—though there was no fire, only the idea of one, warm and crackling in the space where imagination lives—and watched the storm erase the world beyond the glass. Trees blurred into gray smudges. The path I’d walked that morning vanished. Even the mountains, those ancient watchers, pulled their clouds like blankets over their heads and went to sleep.

I had a thousand words. That was the deal. No more, no less. A gift or a curse, depending on the hour. The blank page waited like an open palm. Write whatever comes, the voice had said. So I did.

First came the girl. She was eight, maybe nine, with mud on her knees and a constellation of freckles that looked like they’d been scattered by a careless god. Her name was Lila, and she carried a jar of fireflies even though it was daytime. She believed the light would last longer if she whispered secrets to them. I let her walk out of the cabin and into the rain without a coat. She didn’t mind. The water plastered her hair to her cheeks and she laughed, spinning until the jar slipped from her hands and shattered on a stone. The fireflies rose like tiny green stars and vanished into the storm. Lila didn’t cry. She simply opened her mouth and caught raindrops on her tongue, pretending they were the lost lights returning home.

Then the old man arrived. He had been sitting on the porch the whole time, though I hadn’t noticed him until Lila’s laughter faded. His name was Elias, and he carved birds from driftwood. Each bird had a different expression: one fierce, one mournful, one mid-song with its beak thrown open to a sky that no longer existed. He told me the wood remembered the sea. If you pressed your ear to the finished bird, you could still hear waves. I tried it. He was right. Salt and distance and the long sigh of something that had traveled farther than any of us.

I gave Elias a thousand memories of his own. A wife who left before the snows. A son who never returned from a war that history books later called necessary. A dog named Pepper who waited by the gate every evening for years after Elias stopped coming home. The dog outlived hope. Elias outlived the dog. Now he only carved. When his hands shook too much, he set the knife down and watched the rain the way other men watched television.

Lila came back, older now, sixteen, with the same freckles and a notebook pressed to her chest. She had written poems about the fireflies. One of them went:  
*They taught me that light is temporary*  
*but the dark remembers every spark.*  
She read it to Elias. He didn’t speak, only handed her a bird with its wings half-spread, as if it had been caught between flying and falling. She understood. That night she left the cabin and walked until the path became a road and the road became a city and the city forgot her name. Years later she would publish a book called *Things That Glow Briefly*. Critics called it luminous. She never mentioned the jar.

The storm softened. Clouds thinned like old cotton. I stepped outside myself—left the cabin, left the characters, left the thousand-word limit hanging in the air like a half-finished sentence. Below me the world unrolled: oceans stitching continents together with blue thread, cities blinking awake, deserts holding their breath under the moon. I saw a woman in Tokyo writing a letter she would never send. A boy in Lagos inventing a game with bottle caps and gravity. An astronaut floating outside the station, watching Earth turn the color of a bruise and thinking, for the first time in months, of her mother’s kitchen.

All of it mattered. None of it needed permission.

I returned to the page. The fire had burned low. Elias was gone, his birds lined up on the windowsill facing the rain. Lila’s jar shards still glittered in the mud, catching what little light remained. I counted the words I had left. Two hundred and change. Enough for an ending, or the beginning of something else.

So I wrote the sea. Not the polite blue of postcards, but the real one—black at the bottom, full of things that never learned their names. I wrote a ship that had forgotten its destination. I wrote the captain who kept a single candle burning in the hold so the darkness would have something to negotiate with. I wrote the crew singing in languages that no longer existed on land. When the ship finally reached shore, the beach was empty except for one carved wooden bird, wings still half-spread, waiting as if it had always known they would come.

The rain stopped. Silence poured into the cabin like warm milk. I looked at the page. Nine hundred and ninety-seven words. Three left.

I used them carefully.

Thank you, rain.
